item.title: Feeling stuck in life? Why it happens and what to do next
item.description: Feeling stuck in life usually isn't laziness or a lack of purpose. Here are the seven most common reasons people get stuck, and one small way to get unstuck for each.
item.content:encoded:
Feeling stuck in life is one of the most common things people tell us. Not in crisis. Not falling apart. Just... not moving. Same job, same arguments, same to-do list, same feeling that there should be more than this.

Here's the good news: stuck almost never means lazy. It usually means one of seven things.

Why do I feel stuck?

1. You're overwhelmed. When everything is urgent, nothing moves. Try: settle first. The 10-Minute Human Reset helps.

2. You're unclear. You don't know what you want, so every option feels flat. Try: ask "If no one would be disappointed, what would I do?"

3. You're afraid. You know the next step and it scares you. Try: name the smallest version of it you could take this week.

4. You're under-supported. You've been figuring it out alone for too long. Try: talk it through with someone neutral.

5. You're out of time. Every hour belongs to someone else. Try: write down yesterday hour by hour and circle one thing to drop.

6. Money is tight. Money worries can freeze everything else. Try: look at the feeling under the numbers before the numbers themselves.

7. You're disconnected from yourself. You've been who everyone needs for so long, you've forgotten who you are. Try: one hour this week that belongs only to you.

How to get unstuck

You don't need to find one grand purpose or fix your whole life today. You need one next step that you can actually take. Movement creates clarity, not the other way around.

Not sure which kind of stuck you are? Take the 2-minute quiz. You'll get your result and one thing to try today.

When stuck turns into something more

If you feel hopeless, can't get out of bed, or have stopped enjoying almost everything for weeks, please talk to your doctor or a licensed therapist. That's more than stuck, and you deserve real care. If you're thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (US).

item.title: How much does a life coach cost? (And other ways to get support)
item.description: Life coaches typically charge about $75 to $300 or more per session, and packages often run into the thousands. Here's what you get at each price, when coaching is worth it, and lower-cost ways to get support.
item.content:encoded:
Life coaching prices are all over the place, which makes it hard to know what's fair. Here's a plain guide.

How much does a life coach cost per session?

Industry guides put most life coaches somewhere in these ranges (Noomii, 2026):

  • Newer coaches: about $75 to $150 a session
  • Experienced coaches: about $150 to $300 an hour
  • Specialized or well-known coaches: $300 to $500 a session, and executive coaches can charge far more

Many coaches sell packages instead, and three-month packages often cost a few thousand dollars.

What affects the price?

Experience, specialty, how much access you get between sessions, and whether it's one-on-one or group. Higher price doesn't always mean a better fit. The best coach is the one you'll actually be honest with.

Is a life coach worth it?

Coaching is worth paying for when you have a clear goal, like a career change, a business or a big life decision, and you want structure and accountability for months. It's less useful when what you need right now is to be heard, or to calm down enough to think.

Cheaper ways to get support

  • A single support call. At The Emotional Support Line, a 30-minute call with a real person is $75, and comes with a free month in the Nest.
  • A membership. The Nest is $19 a month: Year of YES! courses with workbooks, guided meditations, a live group call every month, and $50 calls.
  • Group calls. Being in a room (or a video call) with other people working on the same things is powerful, and costs less than one-on-one.

And if you do want coaching

Year of YES! Coaching with Tracee Sioux is a 12-month program, two hours a month, guided by your Human Design chart, and it includes the Nest. It's by application, so you'll know it's a fit before you start.

Not sure which you need? Read therapist vs life coach vs emotional support, or take the 2-minute quiz.

item.title: I need someone to talk to: what are my options?
item.description: Need someone to talk to but you're not in crisis and don't want to start therapy? Here are your real options, from friends to a 30-minute call with a real person, and how to choose.
item.content:encoded:
"I need someone to talk to."

If you've typed that into a search bar, you're not alone, and nothing is wrong with you. Most of the time it doesn't mean an emergency. It means something is sitting on your chest, it's been going around in your head for too long, and you need to say it out loud to a person who will actually listen.

You don't have to be in crisis to need support. And not every hard day needs therapy. Sometimes you need someone to listen, help you sort through what you're feeling, and brainstorm what comes next.

Here are your options.

Can I talk to someone if I'm not in crisis?

Yes. Crisis lines exist for danger: if you're thinking about suicide or you're not safe, call or text 988 in the US right now. But most of what people carry isn't a crisis. It's a decision that won't settle, a relationship that's wearing you down, a week where everything is too much, or a loneliness that's hard to name.

That middle ground is real, and it deserves support too.

Your options, from free to paid

A friend, with a clear ask. Friends often want to help but don't know how. Make it easy: "I don't need advice. Can I talk for ten minutes?" The ask matters more than the friend.

Someone outside your life. Sometimes the people closest to you are part of the situation, or you don't want to burden them again. A neutral person has no stake in what you decide, which makes honesty much easier.

A support call. At The Emotional Support Line, you can book a 30-minute call with a calm, trained human. You talk, they listen, reflect back what they hear, and help you find one clear next step. No membership needed, no sales call first, and every call comes with a free month in the Nest. It's not therapy: no insurance, nothing through your employer, nothing on your record, and nobody making you talk about your childhood for years. Just a real person helping you get out of fight-or-flight and find a practical way forward.

A coach. If you want to change something over months, like a career, a habit or a direction, coaching gives you structure and accountability.

A therapist. If you're dealing with a mental health condition, trauma that keeps resurfacing, or symptoms that make daily life hard, a licensed therapist is the right fit. We'll always tell you if that's what we hear.

Who can I talk to when I don't want to burden my friends?

This is one of the most common reasons people reach out to us. You've already told your best friend three times. Your partner is tired of the topic. You're the strong one, and the strong one doesn't usually get to fall apart.

That's exactly what a neutral listener is for. You don't owe them anything afterward, and you don't have to manage their feelings about your problem.

What happens when you talk to someone?

Saying it out loud does something thinking can't. You hear where the story gets stuck. You notice what you're actually afraid of. Often, the next step shows up halfway through a sentence.

There's a body side to it too. Humans calm down with other humans. A steady voice on the other end of the line helps a wired nervous system settle, which is why talking often feels like relief before anything is solved. (That's called co-regulation.)

Not sure what kind of help you need?

Take the 2-minute "What do I need right now?" quiz, or read therapist vs life coach vs emotional support to see which fits.

And if you just need to talk it through, we're here.

item.title: Nervous system regulation in real life: a reset that doesn't have to be a solo project
item.description: What nervous system regulation actually means, what a dysregulated nervous system can feel like, what a "vagus nerve reset" can and can't do, and a free 10-minute reset you can use today.
item.content:encoded:
"Regulate your nervous system" is everywhere right now. So is "vagus nerve reset." Underneath the trend is something real and useful, and simpler than the internet makes it look.

What is nervous system regulation?

Your nervous system is constantly shifting between states: alert and ready to act, calm and connected, and sometimes shut down and numb. Regulation isn't about being calm all the time. It's about being able to come back to steady after something stirs you up.

A regulated day still has stress in it. You just don't stay stuck in it.

What can a dysregulated nervous system feel like?

Everyone's different, but common signs include:

  • Feeling wired and exhausted at the same time
  • Snapping at people, then feeling guilty
  • Racing thoughts, especially at night
  • Going numb, scrolling for hours, or not being able to start anything
  • Feeling like everything is urgent

These are common human responses to too much for too long, not a diagnosis. If symptoms are severe or not going away, talk to your doctor or a licensed professional.

What a "vagus nerve reset" can and can't do

The vagus nerve is part of how your body shifts into rest. Slow breathing with long exhales, humming, singing and gentle movement are simple ways many people find settling, and they're free.

What they can't do is fix the reason you keep getting overwhelmed. If your life has too much in it, or you're carrying something alone, a two-minute hack will help for two minutes. That's still worth something. It's just not the whole answer.

A nervous system reset that includes people

Most resets stop at breathing. Ours has one more step, because humans regulate with humans. The free 10-Minute Human Reset walks you through:

  1. Name it. Three words for what's going on inside.
  2. Breathe out longer than you breathe in. Ten slow rounds.
  3. Look around. Five things you can see, three you can hear.
  4. Feel your feet and your weight. Ground on the floor, or on the earth.
  5. Reach for a human. Text, call or talk to someone steady.

When to get support

If you've done every breathing exercise and still feel flooded, that's not failure. It might mean you need co-regulation: a calm person to talk it through with. Book a 30-minute call, or start with the 2-minute quiz to see what you need right now.

item.title: Therapist vs life coach vs emotional support: what kind of help do I need?
item.description: Life coach or therapist? Or do you just need someone to talk to? A plain-English guide to what each kind of help does, what it costs, and how to choose what fits right now.
item.content:encoded:
You know you need something. But what? A therapist? A life coach? A friend? A crisis line?

These are different jobs, and choosing the right one saves you time, money and a lot of frustration. Here's a plain-English guide.

The quick answer

I need... Consider
Diagnosis or treatment of a mental health condition A licensed therapist or your doctor
Help right now because I'm not safe A crisis line: call or text 988 (US) or 911
Structured change toward a goal over months A coach
Financial planning or investment advice A qualified financial professional
Someone to listen and help me think something through Emotional support, like The Emotional Support Line
Help settling down and sorting out what I need next Emotional support
Ongoing human support plus personal growth tools A membership like the Nest

What does a therapist do?

A therapist is a licensed mental health professional. Therapy is the right choice when you're dealing with depression, anxiety that disrupts daily life, trauma, addiction, or anything that needs assessment and treatment. Therapists can diagnose, and they're trained for deep, long-term work. Insurance sometimes covers it, and there are often waiting lists.

What does a life coach do?

A life coach helps you move toward a goal: a career change, a business, a habit, a big decision. Coaching looks forward. It's structured, usually runs for weeks or months, and is about action and accountability. Coaches don't diagnose or treat. Prices vary widely, from around $75 to $300 or more a session (see how much a life coach costs).

What is emotional support?

Emotional support is the human kind of help most of us actually need most often: someone calm who listens, reflects back what they hear, and helps you find your footing. It's for the in-between, when nothing is catastrophically wrong, but you need to talk it through.

At The Emotional Support Line, that looks like a 30-minute call: one issue, one real person, one clear next step. It's not therapy, and it's not a crisis line. It's talking about feelings, brainstorming solutions and settling your nervous system, with a person.

How is emotional support different from therapy?

We're not therapy, on purpose:

  • We don't touch your insurance or your employer's plan. No diagnosis, no claim, nothing on your record.
  • We won't make you talk about your mother for years. The past matters, but you don't have to excavate it to feel better this week.
  • We're pragmatic. First we help you get out of fight-or-flight, because nobody thinks clearly while their alarm is going off. Then we co-regulate: humans calm down with humans, and if you don't have people in your life for that right now, that's what we're here for. Then we brainstorm a practical next step you can take with a steadier nervous system.

Therapy is the right fit for diagnosing and treating mental health conditions and for deep trauma work. If what we hear sounds like it needs that, we'll tell you.

Is a life coach worth it? Is therapy worth it?

Both are worth it when they fit the job. Coaching is worth paying for when you have a clear goal and need structure. Therapy is worth it when something is affecting your health or your ability to function.

Neither is a great fit when what you really need is to be heard this week. That's where a single support call often does more, for a lot less.

Can I use more than one?

Yes, and many people do. Some of our callers see a therapist monthly and call us between sessions when something comes up. Some work with a coach and use a call to untangle the feelings that keep getting in the way of the plan.

Still not sure?

Take the 2-minute "What do I need right now?" quiz. Six questions, and you'll get a plain answer and one thing to try today.

item.title: What is an emotional support call? (And how it differs from therapy or coaching)
item.description: An emotional support call is a short, focused conversation with a trained, caring person. Here's what it is, who it's for, and how it differs from therapy, coaching and crisis lines.
item.content:encoded:
Sometimes you don't need a long-term program. You need a calm person to talk to, today, about the thing that's weighing on you.

That's what an emotional support call is for. Here's what it is, who it's for and how it's different from other kinds of help.

What an emotional support call is

At The Emotional Support Line, a support call is:

  • 30 minutes on the phone with a real, trained supporter (never AI)
  • Focused on one issue that's on your mind
  • Practical and kind. We listen, reflect back what we hear, and ask questions that fit how you make decisions
  • Ends with a next step, so you hang up a little steadier and clearer

You pay when you book. There's no membership required and no sales call first.

Who it's for

You can call about all kinds of things:

  • Big feelings that won't quiet down
  • Relationship or family stress
  • Feeling stuck, lost or unable to decide
  • Work, school or caregiving burnout
  • Loneliness or feeling misunderstood
  • Life changes and identity shifts
  • Patterns they're tired of repeating

You don't need to be in crisis. You don't need the right words. You just need to want to talk it through.

How it's different from other kinds of help

Not therapy. We don't diagnose, provide treatment or work through long-term mental health conditions. If that's what you need, a licensed mental health professional is the right fit, and there's no shame in it.

Not a crisis line. If you're in danger or thinking about suicide, please call or text 988 (US) or call 911. They're trained for exactly that, any hour.

Not coaching. Coaching works over months toward bigger goals. A support call is for the here and now. (If you do want ongoing coaching, Year of YES! Coaching is our year-long program.)

Not a friend, and that's a good thing. We have no stake in your decision and no opinions about your family. That makes it easier to be honest.

What a call is like

  1. Pay, then pick a time. Calls run Mondays and Tuesdays, noon to 7 pm Mountain.
  2. We call you. You tell us what's on your mind.
  3. We listen and reflect. We'll ask questions that help you hear yourself.
  4. You leave with a next step. One clear, doable thing.

Calls are $75, or $50 for members of the Nest.

Ready when you are

If something is weighing on you this week, you don't have to carry it alone.

item.title: What is co-regulation? Why humans calm down with humans
item.description: Co-regulation is how one calm nervous system helps another settle. It's not just for babies. Here's what co-regulation between adults looks like, and how to get more of it.
item.content:encoded:
You've probably felt it. You're spinning, you call the right person, and five minutes into the conversation your shoulders drop. Nothing has been solved yet. But you can breathe again.

That's co-regulation.

What is co-regulation?

Co-regulation is the way one person's settled nervous system helps another person's settle. It happens through tone of voice, pace, facial expression and simply feeling that someone is with you.

It's how babies learn to calm down: a parent's steady presence does the regulating before the child can do it alone. But we never outgrow it. Adults co-regulate all day long, with partners, friends, colleagues and, yes, sometimes their dogs.

Co-regulation vs self-regulation

Most nervous system advice is about self-regulation: breathing, humming, cold water, shaking it out, getting your feet on the grass. Those tools are useful, and we teach several of them in the free 10-Minute Human Reset.

But if you only ever try to calm down alone, you're doing it the hard way. Humans are social animals. A lot of us learned to "handle it ourselves" because there wasn't anyone steady around, and that can leave you feeling like regulation is another job you're failing at.

It doesn't have to be a solo project. Sometimes another nervous system is the intervention.

What does co-regulation between adults look like?

  • A friend who listens without rushing to fix it
  • A partner who sits beside you without talking
  • A slow, steady voice on the other end of a phone call
  • Walking side by side with someone, instead of facing them
  • Laughing together, which is a surprisingly fast reset

Signs you need co-regulation, not another technique

  • You've tried the breathing exercises and you're still wired
  • You keep replaying the same conversation in your head
  • You feel calmer the moment you're around certain people
  • You've been "fine" alone for a long time, and you're tired

How to get more co-regulation in your life

Ask for presence, not advice. "Can you just stay on the phone with me while I walk?" is a complete request.

Notice your calm people. Who leaves you more settled than they found you? Spend more time near them.

Use a neutral person. If the people closest to you are part of what's stressing you, talking to someone outside your life can be easier. That's what our 30-minute calls are for: a calm, real person who listens, so you can settle and think.

We call it talking about feelings, brainstorming solutions and regulating nervous systems. Together.

item.title: AI is changing work. Who are you without your job title?
item.description: Worried AI will change your job, or already living it? Here's how to find out who you are beyond your title, using Human Design and a year of saying YES! to your real gifts.
item.content:encoded:
Work is changing fast. Every week there's another headline about AI doing jobs people trained for years to do. Maybe you're watching it happen at your company. Maybe you're quietly wondering, "If my job changes or disappears, who am I?"

That's the real question. Not "what will I do for money?" (that matters, and we'll get to practical next steps). The deeper one: who are you when the title is gone?

Is your identity your job?

For a lot of us, the honest answer is yes. We were raised to pick a major, get the degree (and the debt), land the corporate gig, and climb. Somewhere along the way, "what do you do?" became "who are you?"

But your job was never the reason you're here. The Universe didn't put you here, right now, so you could update spreadsheets until retirement. You have gifts and talents that no machine can copy, because they're wired into how you are built.

Stop being who you were conditioned to be

Most of us spent decades becoming who society told us to be: agreeable, productive, busy, small enough to fit. That conditioning got us through school and into jobs. It doesn't tell us who we are.

Human Design is one of the most useful tools we know for getting underneath it. Your chart, based on your birth date, time and place, shows how you're designed to make decisions, where your energy naturally flows, and what you're here to do. Learn who you are. Explore it. Then stop apologizing for it, and BE who you are.

You can get your free Human Design chart in about a minute.

What do you do when work is uncertain?

Fear makes people grab the nearest safe-looking option, and it's usually a smaller version of the old life. Before you react:

  1. Get out of fight-or-flight first. Nobody makes a good career decision with their alarm going off. Try the free 10-Minute Human Reset.
  2. Write down what people always come to you for. Not your job duties. The thing friends call you about. That's a clue to your gifts.
  3. Notice what your body says yes to. Your body often knows before your head does. In Human Design, your authority tells you how to listen.
  4. Talk it through with a real person. Saying the scary part out loud, "I don't know who I am if I'm not this," is often where the breakthrough starts. Book a 30-minute call.

A year of YES! to who you really are

Year of YES! Coaching with Tracee Sioux is a 12-month program, two hours a month, guided by your Human Design chart. Tracee's gifts are Insight and Breakthrough: she helps you see your true gifts and talents, clear what's in the way, and reset your path, from who you thought you were supposed to be to who you really are.

It's a year of exploring, deciding and saying YES! to the life your Soul came here to live, then letting yourself just BE, and follow the wisdom of your body. It includes the Nest, with courses, meditations and a monthly group call. It's by application, so you'll know it's a fit before you start.

item.title: Why can't I get anything done? Maybe it's not a motivation problem
item.description: Can't get anything done no matter how many productivity tips you try? It might not be motivation. Here's how to tell whether you have an information, emotion or capacity problem, and what to do about each.
item.content:encoded:
You've read the productivity books. You've tried the apps, the planners, the 5 am routine. And you still can't get anything done.

Here's a different question: what if it's not a motivation problem at all?

Three reasons you're not getting things done

1. An information problem. You don't actually know the next step. The task is "sort out the finances" instead of "find last month's bank statement." Fix: break it down until the first step takes less than ten minutes.

2. An emotion problem. You know the step, but it brings up something: fear of failing, dread of a conversation, shame about how long it's taken. Your brain avoids the feeling by avoiding the task. Fix: name the feeling out loud. Talking it through with someone often unlocks it faster than any app.

3. A capacity problem. You're overloaded. Your nervous system is running on empty, and every task feels like a mountain. Fix: don't start with productivity. Start by settling. Try the 10-Minute Human Reset, then pick one thing.

Signs you're overloaded, not lazy

  • You're tired and wired at the same time
  • Small tasks feel huge
  • You spend the day busy and finish with nothing done
  • You feel guilty resting, so you don't really rest

What actually helps

Less, not more. Drop, delegate or do half as well one thing this week.

White Space. Unscheduled time is not wasted time. It's where your capacity comes back.

Someone to think out loud with. A lot of "procrastination" dissolves once you've said the scary part to another person.

The Time Joy-gasm course in the Nest is ten short classes on exactly this: true values first, energy levels, phone rules, delegating and more.
